Description
VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) on-prem has a security issue where this issue may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host. Successful exploitation may compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the orchestrator and data managed by the orchestrator.
On an affected system, any authenticated user can gain operator privileges and masquerade as a local “superuser operator” user. This includes access to functionality that is intended for internal use only and which is not intended to be remotely accessible.
Hosted, including Dedicated, versions of VCO were impacted and have already been patched.
This issue was detected by Arista and is known to be actively exploited.

Required Configuration for Exploitation
VCO is exposed by default. A successful attack requires network access to the VCO web interface and a valid authenticated session on the VCO portal. The minimum user role required is
Enterprise Read Only
, the lowest built-in tenant role. There is no configuration that can prevent the exposure.
Indicators of Compromise
Operators should review VCO web access logs for unexpected activity. Requests containing unusual URL-like path components, encoded characters, references to local or internal services, or high request rates should be investigated.
The following IP addresses have been observed conducting the attacks. It is advised to block these IPs and review logs to see if they are present:
74.82.197.86
38.54.50.151
If compromise is suspected, operators should preserve VCO web access logs, backend application logs, system logs, database logs, and relevant file-system timestamps before remediation where operationally feasible.
Mitigation
The recommended resolution is to upgrade to a fixed VCO release as soon as it is available. For VCOs which are not on a supported release train, customers can contact TAC to discuss possible upgrade options for your release.
Until the fixed software is deployed, operators should apply defense-in-depth controls appropriate for their environment:
Restrict access to the VCO web interface to trusted administrative networks.
Monitor the VCO for accesses from known malicious source IPs.
Monitor for unexpected outbound network activity from the VCO host.
Consider blocking outbound ports not needed for normal activities.
Monitor for backdoor daemons and webshells.
Review recent administrator activity for unexpected changes.
Resolution
The recommended resolution is to upgrade to a fixed VCO release at your earliest convenience.

Impact
Users of Nextcloud with
Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server
app can be vulnerable through proxy.php. A request can cause an operating system command to run as the web server user.
The attack only works while the built-in CODE server is not running. So on a container restart, an upgrade, or after a crash. It is not sufficient to disable the app to avoid the problem, it must be upgraded to >= 26.4.303 or removed.
Users of EOL Nextcloud <= 29 should upgrade their Nextcloud or remove this app.
Standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected.
This is not the same path as CVE-2025-66208, and the fix for that issue does not prevent it.
Patches
The bug was fixed in Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server (richdocumentscode) release 26.4.303.

Exploitability Metrics
Attack Vector:
This metric reflects the context by which vulnerability exploitation is possible. This metric value (and consequently the resulting severity) will be larger the more remote (logically, and physically) an attacker can be in order to exploit the vulnerable system. The assumption is that the number of potential attackers for a vulnerability that could be exploited from across a network is larger than the number of potential attackers that could exploit a vulnerability requiring physical access to a device, and therefore warrants a greater severity.
Attack Complexity:
This metric captures measurable actions that must be taken by the attacker to actively evade or circumvent existing built-in security-enhancing conditions in order to obtain a working exploit. These are conditions whose primary purpose is to increase security and/or increase exploit engineering complexity. A vulnerability exploitable without a target-specific variable has a lower complexity than a vulnerability that would require non-trivial customization. This metric is meant to capture security mechanisms utilized by the vulnerable system.
Attack Requirements:
This metric captures the prerequisite deployment and execution conditions or variables of the vulnerable system that enable the attack. These differ from security-enhancing techniques/technologies (ref Attack Complexity) as the primary purpose of these conditions is not to explicitly mitigate attacks, but rather, emerge naturally as a consequence of the deployment and execution of the vulnerable system.
Privileges Required:
This metric describes the level of privileges an attacker must possess prior to successfully exploiting the vulnerability. The method by which the attacker obtains privileged credentials prior to the attack (e.g., free trial accounts), is outside the scope of this metric. Generally, self-service provisioned accounts do not constitute a privilege requirement if the attacker can grant themselves privileges as part of the attack.
User interaction:
This metric captures the requirement for a human user, other than the attacker, to participate in the successful compromise of the vulnerable system. This metric determines whether the vulnerability can be exploited solely at the will of the attacker, or whether a separate user (or user-initiated process) must participate in some manner.
Vulnerable System Impact Metrics
Confidentiality:
This metric measures the impact to the confidentiality of the information managed by the VULNERABLE SYSTEM due to a successfully exploited vulnerability. Confidentiality refers to limiting information access and disclosure to only authorized users, as well as preventing access by, or disclosure to, unauthorized ones.
Integrity:
This metric measures the impact to integrity of a successfully exploited vulnerability. Integrity refers to the trustworthiness and veracity of information. Integrity of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM is impacted when an attacker makes unauthorized modification of system data. Integrity is also impacted when a system user can repudiate critical actions taken in the context of the system (e.g. due to insufficient logging).
Availability:
This metric measures the impact to the availability of the VULNERABLE SYSTEM resulting from a successfully exploited vulnerability. While the Confidentiality and Integrity impact metrics apply to the loss of confidentiality or integrity of data (e.g., information, files) used by the system, this metric refers to the loss of availability of the impacted system itself, such as a networked service (e.g., web, database, email). Since availability refers to the accessibility of information resources, attacks that consume network bandwidth, processor cycles, or disk space all impact the availability of a system.

Regexp compilation fixes related to GitLab's CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264
Posted by
k0kubun
on 23 Oct 2026
We have released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13. They fix several bugs in Ruby’s regular expression engine (Onigmo) that GitLab found could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab published four CVEs for these issues, and the Ruby releases contain the fixes for the underlying bugs in Ruby.
Background
GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as patterns in CI configuration, with
Regexp.new
. GitLab found that specially crafted patterns could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles them, and that this could be turned into remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab addressed these issues in its own releases by patching the Ruby it ships, and assigned the following CVE identifiers:
CVE-2026-89078
: Double Free issue in Regular Expression Parser (
GitLab 19.4.1
)
CVE-2026-93577
: Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler (
GitLab 19.4.1
)
CVE-2026-97229
: Integer Overflow issue in CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler (
GitLab 19.4.2
)
CVE-2026-110264
: Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler (
GitLab 19.5.1
)

Who is affected
These bugs are reached only when an application compiles a regular expression from a string that an attacker controls, for example by passing it to
Regexp.new
,
Regexp.union
or
Regexp.compile
, or by interpolating it into a regexp literal such as
/#{input}/
. Applications that only use regular expressions written by their own developers are not affected.
Regexp.timeout
does not protect against these bugs. Limiting the length of patterns does not reliably protect against them either, because some of them can be triggered by short patterns.
Recommended action
We recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later.
If you cannot upgrade, please avoid compiling regular expressions from untrusted input.
Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase, in which we normally release only fixes for vulnerabilities. Ruby 3.3.13 includes these fixes as an exception, because GitLab assigned CVEs to issues that rely on them.
About CVE identifiers
We have not requested CVE identifiers in Ruby for these fixes, at least for now.
Ruby has generally considered it unsafe to compile and use a regular expression created from untrusted input. We stated this in the advisory for
CVE-2022-28738
, where we nevertheless treated a double free in Regexp compilation as a vulnerability after a comprehensive assessment. We did the same for
CVE-2024-27282
.
However, the
Regexp documentation
currently discusses untrusted patterns only in terms of denial of service, and recommends a timeout for them. It does not clearly say whether compiling an untrusted pattern is a use case that Ruby supports. We plan to discuss how to document this, and whether we treat this kind of issue as a vulnerability in Ruby, including whether to request CVE identifiers for these fixes. If we request any, we will update this page.
In the meantime, please refer to GitLab’s CVE identifiers listed above when you track these issues, for example in a security scanner.

Backwards incompatible changes
¶
Python 3.10
¶
Pillow has dropped support for Python 3.10,
which reached end-of-life in October 2026.
Saving I mode images as PNG
¶
In order to fit the 32 bits of I mode images into PNG, when PNG images can only contain
at most 16 bits for a channel, Pillow has been clipping the values. Rather than quietly
changing the data, this is now removed. Instead, the image can be converted to another
mode before saving:
from
PIL
import
Image
im
=
Image
.
new
(
"I"
,
(
1
,
1
))
im
.
convert
(
"I;16"
)
.
save
(
"out.png"
)
Image.fromarray mode parameter
¶
Using the
mode
parameter in
fromarray()
was deprecated in
Pillow 11.3.0. In Pillow 12.0.0, this was partially reverted, and now the only
functionality removed is when the mode changes data types. Since pixel values do not
contain information about palettes or color spaces, the parameter can still be used to
place grayscale L mode data within a P mode image, or read RGB data as YCbCr for
example. If omitted, the mode will be automatically determined from the object’s shape
and type.
Image.Image.get_child_images()
¶
Image.Image.get_child_images()
has been moved to
ImageFile.ImageFile.get_child_images()
. The method uses an image’s file pointer,
and so child images could only be retrieved from an
PIL.ImageFile.ImageFile
instance.
Image._show
¶
Image._show
has been removed. Use
show()
instead.
ImageCms.ImageCmsProfile.product_name and .product_info
¶
ImageCms.ImageCmsProfile.product_name
and the corresponding
.product_info
attributes have been removed. They were set to
None
since Pillow
2.3.0.
ExifTags.IFD.Makernote
¶
ExifTags.IFD.Makernote
has been removed. Instead, use
ExifTags.IFD.MakerNote
.
Deprecations
¶
IM image format
¶
The IM image format has been deprecated and removal is planned in Pillow 15.0.0
(2028-10-15). If you are using this format and would like to continue doing so,
open an issue about what other software uses it.
JpegImageFile.load_djpeg
¶
JpegImageFile.load_djpeg
has been deprecated, and will be removed in Pillow 14
(2027-10-15).
Use the built-in JPEG decoder instead, or call
djpeg
directly and decode the
resulting image with Pillow.
ImageQt align8to32()
¶
ImageQt.align8to32()
has been deprecated. This was an undocumented helper function
intended for internal use, so there is no replacement.
API changes
¶
ImageColor.getcolor() with premultiplied alpha modes
¶
When
mode
is
RGBa
or
La
,
getcolor()
now returns
color values premultiplied by the alpha channel, matching how pixels are stored in
those modes. Previously, the unmultiplied values were returned.
Duplicate TIFF tags
¶
If a TIFF IFD contains the same tag more than once, the first value is now kept.
Previously, the last value overwrote the earlier ones.
Saving small ICO images
¶
When saving an image smaller than 16x16 pixels as an ICO without a
sizes
argument, the image’s own size is now used. Previously, none of the default sizes
matched, and an ICO containing no images was written. If no size in
sizes
fits
within the image, a
ValueError
is now raised.
API additions
¶
New resizing filters
¶
Two new filters are available for
resize()
and
thumbnail()
:
Image.Resampling.MKS2013
and
Image.Resampling.MKS2021
. These are versions of the Magic Kernel Sharp filter.
Added
strip_namespaces
argument to
Image.getxmp()
¶
getxmp()
now accepts an optional keyword argument of
strip_namespaces
. It is set to
True
by default, stripping each tag’s XML
namespace URI prefix as before. If set to
False
, each tag’s full
{namespace-uri}local-name
form is kept instead, avoiding collisions between tags
that share a local name across different namespaces.
Added
escape
argument to
PSDraw.text()
¶
text()
now accepts a keyword-only boolean argument,
escape
. Set it to
True
to escape backslashes, for example in Windows paths.
The default,
False
, preserves the existing handling of backslashes and PostScript
escape sequences.
ImageOps invert, posterize and solarize of P images
¶
invert()
,
posterize()
and
solarize()
now support P mode images. The operation is applied
to the palette colors, leaving any alpha values in the palette unchanged. Previously,
these functions raised
NotImplementedError
for P mode.
Path-like objects for font files
¶
load()
,
load_path()
and
save()
now accept
os.PathLike
objects,
such as
pathlib.Path
, in addition to strings.
Other changes
¶
Python 3.15
¶
Pillow 12.3.0 had wheels built against Python 3.15 beta, available as a preview
to help projects prepare for 3.15, and to ensure Pillow could be used
immediately at the release of 3.15.0 final (2026-10-01,
PEP 790
).
Pillow 13.0.0 now officially supports Python 3.15.
Faster import
¶
Importing Pillow takes around half the time it did in Pillow 12.3.0.
PIL.Image
no
longer imports
logging
, modules that are only needed for some operations, such as
tempfile
, are now imported on first use, and on Python 3.15 Pillow also declares
__lazy_modules__
to defer its remaining standard library imports (
PEP 810
). On an
Apple Silicon Mac,
from
PIL
import
Image
took 24 ms on Python 3.14 and 23 ms on
Python 3.15 with Pillow 12.3.0, and now takes 12 ms and 10 ms.
PyPy 3.12
¶
Wheels are now also built for PyPy 3.12, in addition to PyPy 3.11.
Faster JPEG 2000, TIFF, FreeType and LittleCMS in macOS and Linux wheels
¶
Several of the libraries bundled in the macOS and Linux wheels were built without
compiler optimisation. The Windows wheels were not affected.
These libraries are now compiled with
-O2
. Compared to Pillow 12.3.0, the wheels
decode JPEG 2000 images 2 to 3 times faster and encode them about twice as fast,
read and write LZW-compressed TIFF images about twice as fast,
render text with
ImageFont
up to 3 times faster, and
apply
ImageCms
transforms up to 3 times faster.
PNG, JPEG, WebP and AVIF are unaffected, as those libraries were already built with
optimisation.
Performance improvements
¶
Building on the optimizations in Pillow 12.3.0, more of the C code has been
restructured so that compilers can vectorize it. Compared to Pillow 12.3.0,
offset()
is up to 46 times faster,
getbbox()
up to 24 times faster,
flipping and rotating by 180 degrees with
transpose()
up to 10 times faster,
filter()
up to 3.5 times faster,
difference()
up to 3 times faster, and converting P and PA
images to RGB and RGBA up to 2.5 times faster. Saving an optimized GIF with a shared
palette is around 6 times faster and uses less memory.
Wheels now use HarfBuzz for hinting
¶
FreeType can use HarfBuzz to work out which glyphs a script covers,
so that its auto-hinter can derive hinting “Blue Zones” for scripts such as Arabic.
Only the Windows wheels were actually built with this support.
The macOS wheels disabled HarfBuzz interoperability outright,
and the Linux wheels left it up to FreeType’s
configure
,
which in turn fell back to loading HarfBuzz by its unversioned name at
runtime.
Since the bundled copy of HarfBuzz is renamed when the wheel is audited and repaired
for distribution, that lookup only succeeded if a separate copy happened to be
installed on the system with the expected name (e.g.
libharfbuzz.so.0
).
All wheels are now linked against the HarfBuzz that Pillow ships,
which may slightly change how text is rendered in scripts that rely on the auto-hinter.
Thread safety for free-threaded Python
¶
Critical sections now protect most operations on core image objects, such as
conversion, pasting, filtering and pixel access, improving thread safety in the
free-threaded build of Python. AVIF decoding also no longer blocks other threads.
Resizing images with alpha
¶
The
reducing_gap
argument to
resize()
is now
applied to RGBA and LA images. Previously, these modes ignored the argument,
including when called by
thumbnail()
, which uses
reducing_gap=2.0
by default.
Preserved transparency when padding or expanding images in ImageOps
¶
pad()
and
expand()
now preserve the
transparency
value from the source image’s
info
dictionary. Transparent
pixels in L, P and RGB images previously became opaque when a border was added.
New palette colors are allocated without using reserved transparency entries.
Fixed reading FITS images with more than 8 bits per pixel
¶
FITS data is big-endian, but Pillow was reading 16-bit and 32-bit integer data, and
32-bit and 64-bit floating point data, in the native byte order. These images now
load with the correct pixel values.
Fixed accuracy of 16-bit image filters and conversions
¶
Applying a kernel filter to an
I;16
image gave incorrect results for pixel values
above 255, and converting an
I;16N
image to
I
or
F
clipped values to 255.
Both now preserve the full 16-bit range.
Saving APNG frames with different palettes
¶
An APNG file can only contain a single palette. When saving P mode frames with
different palettes, the image is now saved as RGB, or RGBA if any palette contains
alpha, instead of writing the later frames with the wrong colors.
Fixed ImageStat variance rounding
¶
Fixed a floating-point rounding error that may have produced a negative variance in
var
.
Fixed ImageChops.offset() for 16-bit images
¶
offset()
now works correctly for 16-bit-per-channel images.
Fixed drawing on I;16B images
¶
When drawing on an
I;16B
image, some drawing methods wrote in the wrong byte order.
All drawing operations now use the byte order of the image mode.
Fixed histograms for masked LA, La and PA images
¶
When
histogram()
was given a mask for a two-band image (LA,
La or PA), the second band was incorrectly derived from the first band of the input
image, rather than the alpha band.
Fixed exporting Arrow arrays from images with non-contiguous rows
¶
Exporting an image as an Arrow array assumed that its rows were contiguous. However,
this was not the case for
images whose rows were padded to an alignment returned incorrect data,
empty images,
images created by
frombuffer()
, and
images memory-mapped from uncompressed files.
These images crashed instead.
Images with rows that are not contiguous now raise a
ValueError
, and the
others are exported correctly.
Fixed combining GIF frames with missing durations
¶
Saving identical consecutive GIF frames no longer raises a
KeyError
when an earlier
frame has no duration and a later frame does.
PNG palettes are no longer padded when saving with the
bits
argument
¶
When saving a
P
mode image as a PNG with the
bits
argument, Pillow used to pad
the
PLTE
chunk with zeroes up to
2
**
bits
entries. The
PLTE
chunk now only
contains as many entries as the image’s palette actually has, matching the behavior
already used when
bits
is not specified.
Restore image position if ImageSequence.all_frames() fails
¶
If processing a frame in
all_frames()
raises an exception,
the given image will now seek back to its original frame.
Clean up TIFF encoders before closing their output files
¶
TIFF saving now explicitly cleans up the libtiff encoder, including when saving
raises an exception. Previously, delayed encoder destruction could access a closed
file descriptor after it had been reused for another file, disturbing that file’s
position or contents.
tobytes()
also now explicitly cleans up its encoder on
both success and failure, rather than relying on object destruction.
Fixed reading PSD layers at the wrong file offset
¶
When seeking to a layer of a PSD image, the pixel data was read from the wrong

Root cause.
When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f  position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.

Impact
Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.
Because the filename is not validated, a leading
-
/
--
is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to
Image.open()
can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.
Potential RCE (verified).
The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's
@
-file syntax: a filename of the form
@<path>
causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from
<path>
, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of
id
).
Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with
-dSAFER
enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)
Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk)
This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this.
Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.

This post focuses on the three critical findings. An attacker could make a Solana payment appear successful without transferring tokens, collect a login signature for an unrelated website, or get an automated client to authorize spending its entire balance of a supported token.
Each issue crossed a different trust boundary: what counted as a payment, which website a signature was for, and who decided how much the wallet could spend.
The findings
A typical x402 exchange involves a client, a server selling a resource, and a facilitator that checks and submits payments. The server supplies payment details, including the amount, token, network, and recipient. The client signs, and the facilitator checks that the payment satisfies those requirements.
That flow needs protection in both directions. A merchant must be able to trust that an accepted payment actually pays them. A client must be able to contact an unfamiliar server without giving it unrestricted control over its wallet.

With an automatic signer and no application-supplied policy, the client could sign that authorization. For a token supporting the signed transfer mechanism, the attacker could submit it and collect the funds. The practical limits were the wallet’s balance and any external signer restrictions.
The HTTP decoding path also parsed payment requirements without calling the existing schema validator. Our local test showed malformed requirements reaching the selector even though that validator would have rejected them. But schema validation alone would not fix the spending issue: a correctly formatted request can still ask for far more money than the client intended to pay.
This made the issue critical for funded automated clients. A single hostile server response could obtain authorization to drain a supported token balance without a separate approval prompt.
Disclosure and fixes
We reported the 3 critical and 13 high severity findings to the x402 team on August 12, 2026. The 3 critical vulnerabilities were fixed by August 20th. A further 9 medium and low severity findings were submitted on September 9th.
The security requirements are straightforward. The Solana verifier should check the instruction type before parsing it as a transfer. The sign-in client should compare the requested domain and URI with the contacted website before signing. Payment clients should validate incoming requirements and enforce explicit per-payment and total budgets, alongside permitted tokens, networks, and recipients.
These checks must run before the client signs or the facilitator accepts a payment. Optional policies only protect applications that actually enable them.
Conclusion
Automatic payments depend on clear limits. A successful transaction must transfer the required funds, a login signature must belong to the website being contacted, and a price supplied by a server must fit the client’s spending policy.

Introduction
Back in October 2022, Kaspersky GReAT was looking into a peculiar advertisement on a hacking forum. A cybercriminal
had been advertising
a UEFI bootkit, dubbed BlackLotus, that could bypass Secure Boot, for $5,000. Given the low price for such powerful capabilities, the cybersecurity community initially took this advertisement with a grain of salt. As no BlackLotus samples were found in the wild, no one could at the time verify the claims made in the forum post.
BlackLotus advertisement
However, about half a year later, in March 2023, ESET
confirmed
that the BlackLotus advertisement was genuine. The researchers tracked down samples of this bootkit and confirmed that it can indeed bypass Secure Boot through a vulnerability called Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894). As this vulnerability was still exploitable in 2023, Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address it.
Since the release of these updates, the BlackLotus bootkit has gone quiet — no publicly known attacks have used it. Yet in early 2026, we discovered a malware sample similar to BlackLotus that was used in an APT campaign in Central Asia. In this report, we share our findings, including new payloads and possible attribution of this campaign.
The return of the infamous bootkit
In early 2026 we identified a complex APT attack targeting diplomatic agencies in Central Asian countries — namely Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This attack involved a UEFI bootkit that we dubbed BlackX. Having examined it, we found it to be similar to BlackLotus.
Attackers have been deploying BlackX after compromising the victim machine networks and obtaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, we observed them dropping the following files:
inst.exe
, an installer executable
PVMDIJGKAX2
, an RC4-encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation
The installer was launched with the command line
C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1
. The last argument here is the RC4 key used for decryption.
Curiously, the file
inst.exe
does not contain any malicious strings or embedded blobs. All the files needed to install the malicious payload are inside
PVMDIJGKAX2
, which makes it harder for incident responders to retrieve the bootkit components.
The installer package drops a set of files to both system and UEFI partitions, designed to exploit the Baton Drop vulnerability. We noted that the implementation of the exploit is remarkably similar to the one used in the BlackLotus malware. As with BlackLotus, the goal of the exploit is to install custom Machine Owner Keys (MOK), which allows loading arbitrary EFI files on the target machines to manipulate Secure Boot.
While the vulnerability exploitation chain was implemented very similarly to BlackLotus, we spotted differences between the exploits in BlackLotus and BlackX. That said, the source code of the BlackLotus bootkit has never been published online. This could mean that the attackers behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the BlackLotus bootkit or purchased its source code from cybercriminals. Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors.
Payload launched by the bootkit
The UEFI payload delivered during the Baton Drop exploitation has a classic bootkit goal — to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. This driver differs from the one deployed by BlackLotus and is signed with a certificate belonging to an organization named 温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室 (English: Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio). At the time of writing, this certificate (serial number: 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072) has been revoked by its issuer.
The driver aims to tamper with security solutions installed on the machine. For example, it disables process, thread, and registry callbacks related to security solutions. It also tampers with ETW providers so that security solutions cannot access their output. Curiously, some of the tampering procedures are designed to run only if Kaspersky or Avast solutions are installed on the infected machine. However, during dynamic analysis of this driver, we found that these procedures are useless — they fail to interfere with Kaspersky products in any way.
The driver also protects the bootkit’s files from tampering. It intercepts kernel requests to open these files and returns a handle to
calc.exe
instead of a malicious file handle.
User-mode second-stage payloads
Apart from tampering with security solutions, the driver also deploys a user-mode payload. We observed two such payloads, used for cyberespionage, in the wild. One of them is a RAT that can load further-stage .NET payloads. This RAT uses cloud storage for C2 server communications — we observed its versions using Google Drive, OneDrive, and Yandex.Disk. Having connected to a cloud storage service, this RAT iterates over files available there and interprets them depending on the file suffix. Below is a list of supported suffixes:

We also observed another payload delivered through the bootkit, which we dubbed OxiDLLRunner. It is a malicious DLL obfuscated with OLLVM. It is loaded by the legitimate file
googleupdate.exe
(original filename:
jcef_helper.exe
, MD5: AF8A983B9ADA07EAE1259BF2953ABD40), which is also delivered by the bootkit. The DLL decrypts the contents of the file
v8_context_snapshot.bin
, which resides in the same folder, and then jumps to the beginning of the decrypted content. The decrypted data starts with shellcode followed by a PE file, which is a Rust payload designed to communicate with the
www[.]archivetj[.]com
C2 server. During communication, this payload is supposed to receive DLL files exporting a function named
create_plugin
, which are then executed in separate threads.
Attribution
Based on the following facts, we have attributed this attack to the APT41 threat actor with medium confidence:
In June 2026, ESET
published a blog post
on attacks by the FishMonger threat actor, which the community assumes to be related to APT41. This post describes a kernel implant with a PDB path starting with C:\Users\
xdd
\Desktop. While describing the campaign, the post also suggests the possible use of an unspecified UEFI bootkit component, which might exploit CVE‑2023‑24932. We observed the identifier “xdd” used multiple times in the BlackX bootkit payloads, so we assess that BlackX is the UEFI bootkit referenced in the ESET blog post;
The payloads deployed by BlackX are loaded using a legitimate executable abused via DLL sideloading, and an encrypted file — this pattern is common among Chinese-speaking threat actors;
The OxiDLLRunner file has been obfuscated with OLLVM, an obfuscator commonly used by Chinese-speaking actors.
Why did the target organizations get infected?
During our initial analysis of BlackX, we thought that attackers succeeded in deploying it due to the negligence of the target organizations. Baton Drop, the vulnerability used to deploy BlackX, was disclosed back in 2023 and was patched, so we first thought that the infected machines lacked the relevant updates. However, our investigation proved this wrong — the targeted machines were fully patched.
Instead, we found out that the problem was with the patch itself. As it turned out, the patch for the Baton Drop vulnerability is designed to revoke the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate used to sign vulnerable UEFI components. However, this revocation does not happen automatically upon patch installation — the user has to
trigger it manually
. This is done with the following steps:
A registry flag is set inside HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Secureboot;
A scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update is created.
This patch is designed to be applied manually — for instance, applying it automatically could break dual-boot systems relying on the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate to load. At the same time, this patch deployment practice creates a problem — as it is extremely unusual for a system administrator to take extra steps after installing an update. Usually, when applying patches, system administrators take no further action unless an installation failure occurs. These instructions for activating the patch are buried deep on the Microsoft website, and we assess that they are quite hard for an average IT administrator to notice.
Curiously,
Microsoft’s plan
for deploying the Baton Drop patches mentions an “Enforcement Phase” that involves revoking the “Windows Production PCA 2011” certificate automatically, without user interaction. At the time of publishing this post, this stage has not been implemented. On October 19, 2026, this certificate expired, but this does not prevent the vulnerable binaries from loading unless the certificate is blocklisted.
It is likely that the threat actor behind this campaign took into account that few organizations realized the importance of manually activating the Baton Drop patch. As such, we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit.
Conclusion
Patch management is important for every organization, as updates from vendors help protect software and hardware against known vulnerabilities. However, sometimes installed patches fail to protect against the flaws they address. The BlackLotus story we described is not the only such example — for instance, in 2025 Microsoft released an update against the
ToolShell vulnerability
that also had to be applied manually.
However, modern security solutions are designed to account for such cases when installed patches fail to protect against security flaws for one reason or another. For instance, the
Exploit Prevention component
available in Kaspersky products prevents exploits from running if the patch is not applied, or if it is a zero-day vulnerability with no available patch. It is thus crucial to equip all machines in an organization with security solutions and constantly monitor the alerts they raise.

Stray Cat, Open Doors: How k0t Wanders Through the Network Edge
Group-IB and NyxLab expose threat actor k0t's large-scale campaign exploiting FortiGate, FortiWeb, and Palo Alto GlobalProtect edge devices to harvest credentials, establish persistent access and exfiltrate data
October 21, 2026 ·
min to read · Threat Intelligence

Introduction
Group-IB
Threat Intelligence
, together with NyxLab, collaborated on a joint investigation on a campaign involving widespread exploitation of network edge devices. This joint-investigation effort has managed to uncover indications that this may be connected to the FortiBleed cluster seen earlier this year in June as well as the exposure of adversarial tooling as well as discovery of Tactics, Techniques and Procedures (TTPs) employed by the threat actor known as ‘k0t’. Notable among the observed TTPs is the exploitation of vulnerabilities in network devices such as FortiGate Firewalls and Palo Alto GlobalProtect to gain initial access. Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration.
From our investigation we also note victim overlaps with several ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, suggesting a possible relationship with ransomware operators or an Initial Access Broker (IAB) role However at this point of the investigation, the relationship between the campaign operators and these ransomware groups, including any direct affiliation, is still unconfirmed.
Due to the large amount of technical information acquired over the course of this investigation, we will be publishing an additional in-depth technical report at a later time.
Key discoveries
Large-scale campaign involving vulnerability exploitation and brute-forcing of exposed network devices
More than 70,000 exposed credentials associated with network devices, LDAP dumps etc. which were not linked to any other threat actors, including the previously reported FortiBleed cluster
Persistent access to corporate networks via OpenConnect VPN as well as installation of Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tools as well as AdaptixC2
Artifacts and ransomware overlaps indicate that this may be an Initial Access operation undertaken by Brokers with association with various ransomware groups.

Victimology
Victims we have observed in this campaign are global and from a wide range of industries. This lack of specificity is likely due to the operators’ chosen reconnaissance approach targeting exposed devices such as FortiGate and FortiWeb firewalls, Palo Alto GlobalProtect etc. as such, any analysis done based on the distribution of victims observed in this campaign is likely a reflection of less than ideally configured network devices that are vulnerable to being discovered using public network scanning tools. We also note that many of the FortiGate compromises are dated between February 2026 and June 2026, a stark overlap in timeline with the widely reported FortiBleed campaign.
Since victim identifiers observed vary from public domains and email addresses to internal IPs, exact victim attribution cannot be verified for the entirety of the observed victim list. However, we note some number of  unique domains mentioned in adversarial operational data, and estimate this to be the lower bound of actual victim organizations affected by this campaign.
Of these unique domains, we note the following geographical distribution.
The Asia Pacific and Latin America regions account for the largest share of unique domains identified in the available dataset. However, this distribution should not be interpreted as evidence of deliberate regional targeting. It may instead reflect the geographic distribution of exposed devices identified through public scanning and access-data services.
Attack Chain
Reconnaissance is conducted through public scanning tools rather than target-specific research. Using the attack-surface search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye, the operators enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances in bulk, filtering candidates by product and exposure to assemble large target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices. The operators then attempt to gain initial access by attempting to exploit vulnerabilities in the exposed appliances or perform brute force attacks. On successful attack additional credential harvesting is performed at the compromised device, and connection to the targets are achieved via OpenConnect VPN connection. At this stage, majority of the devices seen being targeted are Fortinet firewalls and Palo Alto GlobalProtect devices/portals.
Figure 1. General attack chain observed by campaign operators.
Once initial access has been gained, the operators continue their intrusion via hands-on-keyboard attacks, undertaking discovery activities, performing additional credential theft and attempting to escalate toward domain-administrator control. To ensure they retain access, they establish persistence by deploying remote-management agents such as MeshAgents to control compromised devices from a central MeshCentral server, as well as other more commonly abused Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) tools such as Atera. Many organizations that have been successfully compromised by the operators in this campaign had data exfiltrated, and have also been listed by various ransomware groups such as
Qilin
and

Reconnaissance
k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations. His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets. The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign.
Attack-surface search engines are central to this approach. In a public forum post, k0t sought either a premium FOFA account or someone who could retrieve IP addresses from FOFA, ZoomEye and Censys on request. He later reported finding partners for FOFA and ZoomEye (Figure 2). He also sought bulk results in ip:port format so that target lists could be processed by automated tools.
Figure 2. k0t requests a premium FOFA account or on-demand IP exports from FOFA, ZoomEye and Censys. In a follow-up post, he says he has found partners for FOFA and ZoomEye.
GlobalProtect portals are the most prominent target in the observed searches. k0t searched for login-page, response-content and certificate characteristics, first in North America and then across Europe and APAC. These broad searches could yield large lists of candidate portals, which he requested in a format suitable for automated checking. He also showed interest in FortiWeb and FortiGate systems, while searches for SonicWall SMA1000 management consoles suggest an additional area of interest. OPNsense appears among the products he checked, and his vulnerability monitoring extended to Cisco ISE. Current available evidence does not indicate a successful SMA1000 compromise by k0t.
k0t did not rely on one source of target data. Besides search-engine exports, public forum posts show him using and endorsing underground services that supply bulk, product-filtered IP lists, which included AccessTracker and FortiSSL. Such services give him another way to obtain candidate devices when a direct search-engine export is unavailable. k0t was also observed participating in a public thread offering Fortinet access, showing interest in ready-made access. However there was no clear indication if any credential was received or used. Once gathered, candidate addresses were sorted by country and combined into lists for further checking.
Figure 3. Under the aliases “Member19” and “CryptoFeel,” the intruder left reviews of test runs of a service that provides IP lists of network devices for use in future attacks.
His own checkers provided another layer of validation. An OPNsense checker compared multiple indicators found on a web panel, including certificate and login-page characteristics, to reduce false positives. A separate FortiGate scanner also tested the reachability of management and SSH services on common and alternative ports. Together with geographic sorting, these tools turned large collections of potential targets into smaller sets for assessment. The following Initial Access section describes the Fortinet and GlobalProtect techniques; discovery of a host alone does not mean it was attacked. Public forum activity also indicates an interest in improving attack automation and tracking newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
Initial Access
FortiGate Security Scanner
Initial access into victims’ corporate networks via FortiGate and FortiWeb devices is achieved primarily via a custom script. This script is self-named ‘FortiGate Security Scanner’ (with the filename ‘fort[.]py and ‘fortnew[.]py’) and is used by the operators to exploit CVE-2025-64446 (for FortiWeb services) as well as brute-forcing (as a fall-back method) exposed Fortinet devices. An additional identifier of ‘BH’ was also contained within the script under the field ‘SCRIPT_DEV’. At this point of the investigations however, we have not been able to identify this developer and determine their relationship with k0t.
SCRIPT_DEV = "BH"
SCRIPT_LOGO = "FortiGate Security Scanner"
SCRIPT_VER = "2025-12-08"
The tool is built for volume and is executed entirely from the command line, it ingests target ip:port (or ip:port:user:pass) as lines within a .txt file, and runs a configurable worker thread pool (the default is 10 although the operator has been observed to run 50 worker threads), and tags each target’s country from a bundled GeoIP database. It carries a hardcoded exclusion list covering the CIS region and other jurisdictions, but this filter can be disabled with the ‘–no-exclude’ flag. We also note that there are several victims from the excluded nations list being compromised using this tool, indicating that this operator may have used this tool in the ‘–no-exclude’ mode.
CVE-2025-64446 Exploitation
For every device in the target list, the tool first attempts to gain initial access via the exploitation of CVE-2025-64446, a relative path traversal vulnerability affecting Fortinet FortiWeb that may allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute administrative commands through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. For each responsive target appliance it issues a crafted request to the ‘/api/v2.0/cmdb/system/admin%3f/../../../../../cgi-bin/fwbcgi’ endpoint. This request contains a forged CGIINFO header that impersonates the built-in admin account ‘prof_admin’, and uses that access to create a new local administrator.

Brute-Forcing
When validation of the newly created account fails, the tool falls back to credential brute-forcing against the FortiGate REST API. When run with a ‘-comb’ flag, the script generates a list of username and login credentials by combining a hardcoded list with an operator supplied wordlist. The resulting wordlist contains common username and passwords such as:
Usernames
admin
fortinet
fgtsecure
sysadmin
etc.
Passwords

fortigate
F0rt!n3t123
P@ssw0rd123
etc.
When a FortiGate lockout response (“code 2”) is detected, the target will be placed in a dictionary called ‘blocked_hosts’ and no further attempts against that host will be attempted for 60 seconds. After this 60 seconds have elapsed, the blocked host will be removed from ‘blocked_hosts’ and added to a retry queue. We would like to note that 60s is the default administrator lockout time for a FortiGate firewall, which indicates that the developer of this tool possesses significant technical knowledge about the FortiGate appliances.
On a successful authentication attempt after vulnerability exploitation or brute-forcing, and if the ‘–parse-configs’ flag is set, the tool downloads the appliance configuration and decrypts its stored secrets locally, using the default FortiOS AES key, to recover LDAP/Active Directory bound credentials, administrator and local-user credentials, and other configuration data. The ‘default FortiOS AES key’ is a known weakness tracked under CVE-2019-6693. Its associated fix is the addition of ‘private-data-encryption’ option to override the usage of this default AES key; if not toggled explicitly, the affected device will fall back to using this known key.
PAN-OS GlobalProtect Exploitation
Threat Intelligence analysts have also observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass vulnerability affecting GlobalProtect portals and gateways on vulnerable PAN-OS configurations where authentication-override cookies and the relevant certificate configuration are enabled, to gain initial access. The operator makes use of a tool (filename ‘exploit_2026_0257[.]py’) with the self-declared descriptor/name ‘CVE-2026-0257 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Scanner + VPN Connect’,  written by a developer named ‘BeiDou’.
#CVE-2026-0257 PAN-OS GlobalProtect Scanner + VPN Connect
#Coded by ./BeiDou
The exploit entails the use of authentication-override cookie forgery, where a forged cookie is created by encrypting the string ‘admin;;Windows;;[TIMESTAMP];0.0.0.0’ (where [TIMESTAMP] is the current UNIX timestamp) with a public key extracted from the target’s TLS certificate. This forged cookie with an empty password is submitted to the GlobalProtect endpoint ‘/ssl-vpn/login.esp’.
A vulnerable device would decrypt this payload using its private key and check for the appropriate session format, but does not validate that the cookie itself is legitimate. Such a device would respond to this forged request and be flagged by the tool for further exploitation. For every vulnerable device, the forged cookie is written into a temporary file, and used to establish a vpn connection via OpenConnect. This is achieved by creating and running a temporary shell script on the operator’s own device.
connect_script = f"""#!/bin/bash
(echo '{operator_sudo_password}'; cat {cookie_file.name}) | \
sudo -S openconnect --protocol=gp --user={username} \
--usergroup=portal:portal-userauthcookie --os=win --background \
{servercert_flag} {url}
rm -f {cookie_file.name}
When run in a –vuln mode, the operator can skip through the mass-scanning process and will be presented with a window for target selection to establish VPN connection.

Post Exploitation
Once initial access has been obtained, the operators have been observed abusing several administrator/pentesting tools to further compromise their victim’s corporate environments. These tools have been observed to be deployed via hands-on-keyboard attacks although an AI pentesting tool was observed to be present among the operator’s exposed tooling, we do not have evidence of its actual deployment against their victims and was likely still in development. Administrator/Pentesting tools observed include:
NetExec
– The operators have been observed using NetExec extensively to perform malicious actions in their victim’s environments. These include, but are not limited to:
Enumeration of SMB hosts, anti-virus inventory, LDAP domain admin groups, files and folders
Extracting secrets from SAM, LSA, LSASS, DPAPI
Remote execution of commands via ‘atexec’ or ‘smbexec’
SoftPerfect
– We have observed the usage of SoftPerfect for discovery, enumerating shares, hosts and services
Impacket
– Various Impacket scripts by the operators in order to:
GetUserSPNs – to extract service-account Kerberos hashes
secretsdump – authenticate as a domain controller using stolen hashes to extract credentials
noPac
– This tool was used to exploit CVE-2021-42278 and CVE-2021-42287 to escalate to Domain Admin and dump domain credentials
Kerbrute
– Used for password-spraying and brute-forcing attacks against the domain controller
PetitPotam
– Seen used to coerce domain controllers into authenticating to the operator’s relay listener (-pipe all), feeding the NTLM-relay-to-ADCS certificate-theft chain that yields the DC machine hash.
Mimikatz
– Seen used to dump cleartext passwords and NTLM hashes from LSASS.
Artifacts also suggest that subsets of the initial access obtained have been consolidated for other operators (for division of labour), and potentially to be sold to ransomware groups.
Persistence
Within the operator’s exposed tooling, we have observed a large variety of persistence techniques and utilities being abused. As was mentioned in previous sections, the operators made use of OpenConnect to establish a foothold on many exposed corporate networks. However, beyond OpenConnect, we have also observed the abuse of MeshAgents (controlled via a MeshCentral panel) as well as AdaptixC2, and many other commonly abused RMM tools such as Atera, Teramind, AnyDesk and ngrok.
MeshCentral
MeshCentral is a legitimate, open-source web-based remote-management platform that has been abused in this campaign to maintain persistent remote access to a compromised endpoint. A central server, called MeshCentral, hosts an administrative web console, with corresponding MeshAgents which are installed on endpoints connecting to that server over HTTPS/WebSocket, giving whoever has access to the MeshCentral server full remote control of each device. Access via MeshCentral includes remote desktop, terminal shell, file transfer etc.
Figure 5. k0t’s MeshCentral login page at mesh[.]buttruyen[.]com.
Compromised devices are grouped into “device groups” corresponding to the compromised corporations, and are divided among three operator accounts. At the time of analysis, we were able to determine 28 active device groups, which contained 84 compromised devices in total beaconing back to the MeshCentral server at mesh[.]buttruyen[.]com. Artifacts also showed 100 other device groups which have since been removed. Notably, the server held no server-side files, indicating the agents were used for live interactive access only (shell and RDP relay) rather than for data transfer, which was handled separately by Rclone.
While the MeshCentral server was located at mesh[.]buttruyen[.]com, the MeshAgents are hosted on another domain, agent[.]afahimsa[.]top. This is likely an attempt by the operators to lower the likelihood of researchers discovering their C2 MeshCentral server. The MeshCentral server is configured with agentAutoApprove, agentAutoCreateDevice, IgnoreAgentHashCheck and agentInviteCodes options enabled so that each successful installation would automatically result in the compromised device being automatically enrolled into the console without any operator intervention.
AdaptixC2
AdaptixC2 is an open-source, modular post-exploitation and adversary-emulation framework consisting of a Go-based team server and a Qt operator client. In this campaign, the operators used it as an additional command-and-control (C2) channel alongside MeshCentral. Windows agents generated through the team server communicate over HTTPS and provide remote shell access, file transfer, tunnelling, and payload execution.
Build notes and a deployment guide recovered from the operators’ tooling exposed details of their AdaptixC2 configuration. The guide instructed the operators to compile AdaptixC2 from its public repository, generate a default self-signed OpenSSL certificate, and edit profile.json to set the listening interface, team-server port, endpoint, and operator accounts. The observed profile retained the default port 4321, used /endpoint as the team-server endpoint, and contained two operator accounts, operator1 and operator2. The operators also created listeners using the following URIs:
/update
/api/v1/check
/uri.php
Operators also loaded the AdaptixC2 Extension-Kit, which is a collection of scripts designed to add essential utilities, and had also compiled AdaptixC2 agents as Windows executables.
The resulting team server was reachable at hxxps://64[.]94[.]85[.]14:4321/endpoint, however, access was restricted to the operators’ source addresses, which likely explains why the service did not appear in internet-wide scan data. The TLS certificate retained the default subject O=Internet Widgits Pty Ltd. Third-party sources also classified the IP address as malicious, supporting our assessment that it hosted active C2 infrastructure.
AdaptixC2 agents were staged on separate infrastructure and delivered as a fake software installer named clear-thinking_61.92.4_INSTALL.exe. We have observed operators using PowerShell scripts to retrieve these agents from hxxp://162[.]33[.]178[.]213:8888/ and hxxps://sthyjk[.]com:8443/ using curl commands. Both locations pointed to the same host, to which an additional domain, alknene[.]shop, also resolved.
The beacons were configured to communicate with:
64[.]94[.]85[.]14:4321
168[.]100[.]11[.]99
Which were hosted by BitLaunch (AS399629), an anonymous VPS provider that accepts cryptocurrency, as were other infrastructure seen in this campaign. The associated domains were registered through Namecheap.
Operator organization
Available evidence associated with the identified MeshCentral and AdaptixC2 infrastructure indicates the likely involvement of multiple operators, suggesting a collaborative operation rather than activity conducted by a single threat actor.  From our investigations into this cluster, we have preliminarily identified the following aliases to be associated with this activity:
k0t – Likely to be one of the main operators in this campaign
CryptoFeel – Potentially an alias of k0t
Scrooge/ScroogeMcDuck – Likely a collaborator, and potentially another alias, several tools seen are likely to have been acquired by Scrooge
Developers mentioned in this report have not been linked directly to the campaign’s operations, and are potentially free-lance developers used by multiple threat actors. As investigations continue, we expect to learn more about how this campaign is managed and organized. Additional information will be provided in updates as they become available.
Conclusion
In the few victims that the operators have managed to compromise sufficiently, we have observed data exfiltration via the cloud storage utility Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives. Many victims seen in this campaign have also been observed to be later listed by ransomware groups, Qilin and the Gentlemen, on their Data Leak Sites (DLS). However, as of now, we have not yet been able to confirm the relationships between k0t and these ransomware groups, but current evidence suggests that the operators are likely to be acting as Initial Access Brokers (IABs).
We have compared the compromised credentials from this activity with that associated with the previously reported FortiBleed cluster and found a negligible overlap in compromised data. This aligns with reports that many operators are likely to be involved in the FortiBleed activity cluster, suggesting that this may be a separate dataset, operator subset, or related access operation within the broader FortiBleed-related activity. Organisations are advised to act on ensuring that any vulnerabilities mentioned in this report are appropriately remedied. Additional information from our ongoing investigations into this activity, including additional technical details, will be included in a further report which will be released in due time.
Context for Organizations within the Asia-Pacific region
Accounts originating from the Asia-Pacific region account for 37.6% of the unique domains identified in the campaign dataset, the largest regional share in this investigation. NyxLab Defender Perspective
The following points translate the campaign evidence into defensive priorities. They are derived from the artifacts described in this report and should not be read as confirmation that every behaviour occurred in every victim environment.
Why detection can be difficult
The intrusion begins on edge appliances where endpoint detection and response telemetry may not be available. Subsequent access through VPN services and legitimate remote-management tools may resemble authorised administrative activity unless network, identity, appliance and endpoint telemetry are correlated.
The use of dual-use tools, including OpenConnect, MeshCentral, Atera, AnyDesk and Rclone, means detections should consider execution context, installation source, operator account, destination infrastructure and timing rather than relying only on tool names.
Threat-hunting priorities
Edge appliances: review unexpected local administrator creation, configuration exports, trusted-host changes, repeated authentication failures, lockout-and-retry patterns, and administration from unusual source addresses.
VPN and identity: review GlobalProtect and other VPN sessions for unusual client characteristics, atypical access paths, newly observed source infrastructure, and accounts used outside normal administrative patterns.
Windows and Active Directory: hunt for NetExec, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam and Mimikatz activity, including credential dumping, service-account Kerberos requests, remote execution, and abnormal domain-controller authentication.
Persistence and command and control: identify unauthorised MeshAgent, MeshCentral, AdaptixC2, Atera, Teramind, AnyDesk and ngrok installations or communications, and validate whether each instance has an approved owner and business purpose.
Exfiltration: investigate unexpected Rclone execution and transfers to cloud-storage services, including Wasabi S3 and MEGA, particularly when preceded by credential access or broad file enumeration.
Business and incident-response implications
A compromise of an internet-facing security appliance should be treated as a potential enterprise credential compromise, not only as an appliance-patching event. Because configuration data may contain LDAP, Active Directory, administrator and local-user secrets, responders should assess downstream identity exposure, rotate affected credentials, revoke active sessions where applicable, and review subsequent access across the environment.
Immediate actions for exposed organisations
Confirm the external exposure and patch status of FortiGate, FortiWeb and Palo Alto GlobalProtect systems, and remove management interfaces from direct internet access where operationally possible.
Review appliance administrator accounts and recent configuration changes, and investigate any account or trusted-host setting that cannot be linked to an authorised change.
Rotate credentials stored on, bound to or administered through potentially affected appliances, prioritising privileged, LDAP and Active Directory accounts.
Search for the network indicators and file hashes in this report, while recognising that the absence of an IOC match does not rule out compromise.
Preserve appliance, VPN, authentication, endpoint, DNS, proxy and firewall telemetry before retention periods expire, and correlate events across these sources to reconstruct

Network Hardening –
threat actors in this campaign relied heavily on discovery of network devices via public tools which are followed by attempts at brute-forcing
Place network management consoles within an internal network and restrict access to trusted administrative networks or VPN connections. This reduces their exposure to internet-wide scanning and requires threat actors to first gain access to the internal network.
Refrain from using common passwords. Organizations are advised to change default passwords as soon as they can and refrain from using passwords which are commonly used in brute-forcing attacks
Increasing login lockout time can also deter threat actors from successfully carrying out a brute-forcing attack. Multiple failed attempts resulting in login lockout status should also be investigated by analysts
Maintain continuous visibility into internet-facing assets.
Group-IB Attack Surface Management
can identify unintentionally exposed administrative panels, VPN portals, and other management interfaces, allowing organizations to remediate unintended exposure before threat actors discover it.
Patch Management –
The operators in this campaign targeted vulnerabilities in network devices for initial access. k0t in particular has also been active on underground forums looking to acquire tools for similar exploits targeting common network devices (such fortigate, cisco, sonicwall etc.) as well as Windows privilege escalation
Ensure that devices in your organization are patched in a timely manner, prioritising internet facing network devices. Proper prioritization of vulnerabilities according to their impact and severity will also help custodians manage limited resources towards remediating more severe vulnerabilities
Frequent vulnerability scanning and asset discovery should also be conducted to discover unknown vulnerabilities that persist in the organization
Protect Stored Appliance Secrets –
In this campaign, the operators downloaded FortiGate configuration files after gaining access and decrypted them offline to recover the credentials stored inside, including LDAP and Active Directory bind accounts, administrator accounts, local users and other configuration data. Because this decryption is performed against a copy of the configuration held by the operator, it is not detectable on the appliance itself and cannot be prevented by access control alone; the protection must be applied to the stored secrets.
Enable the ‘private-data-encryption’ setting on FortiGate appliances and supply an operator-defined key. FortiGate configuration files are encrypted with a default, publicly known AES key unless this setting is explicitly enabled. If it is not toggled on, the appliance falls back to the known key and any obtained configuration can be decrypted by anyone who holds it. This is tracked as CVE-2019-6693 and is the specific weakness the operators in this campaign exploited at scale.
Treat any FortiGate whose configuration has been exposed as a credential disclosure event, not only as an appliance compromise. Configuration data commonly contains LDAP and Active Directory bind passwords in a recoverable form. Rotate every credential referenced in an affected configuration, including service and bind accounts that may not appear in routine password rotation schedules.
Audit LDAP and directory bind accounts used by edge appliances. These accounts are frequently service accounts with broad read access to the directory, are rarely covered by MFA, and are often excluded from routine password rotation. Where the appliance supports it, use a dedicated low-privilege bind account rather than a domain administrator or equivalent.
Enforce Strict MFA –
Apply Multi-Factor Authentication universally to all accounts where applicable to minimize the threat of stolen plaintext passwords.
Enhance Threat Detection and Response –
Organizations should maintain visibility across endpoint, network, identity, and other relevant telemetry to identify malicious activity following the compromise of internet-facing appliances.
